---
title: "Distillation"
description: "A training approach that transfers behaviour from a larger teacher model to a smaller student model."
term: "Distillation"
letter: "D"
category: "Model Optimization"
difficulty: "Advanced"
---

## Simple explanation

Distillation trains a smaller student model to imitate useful behaviour
from a larger teacher model. The goal is often to reduce inference cost
or make a model easier to deploy.

## Technical explanation

Knowledge distillation may train a student using teacher logits,
probabilities, intermediate representations, or generated examples, in
addition to or instead of ground-truth labels. A temperature parameter
can soften probability distributions. Distillation methods differ in
what signals they transfer and what capabilities they preserve.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Smaller models can reduce latency, memory, or serving cost. Distillation
can help retain some teacher performance, but the student may lose
capabilities or inherit teacher errors and biases.

## How it works

The teacher produces targets for training examples. The student is
optimized to match those targets, often with a distillation loss combined
with the task's original supervised loss. The student must then be
evaluated independently on the intended tasks and deployment conditions.

## Practical example

A team can use a larger text classifier to generate soft class scores,
then train a smaller classifier to match those scores and compare its
accuracy, calibration, and latency on held-out data.

## Common misconceptions

- A student does not automatically inherit every capability of its
  teacher.
- Distillation is not simply shrinking model weights; it involves a
  training objective or transfer process.
- Lower latency or size does not establish that the student is safe or
  suitable for deployment.
